newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenyan maize output set to fall 18 pct in 1996/97.
newsitem.headline: Kenyan maize output set to fall 18 pct in 1996/97.

text.p: Kenya's maize production is forecast to fall 18 percent in 1996/97 (October/September) compared to the previous year, U.N. food agencies said on Thursday.
The U.N. World Food Programme and Food and Agricultural Organisation said in a joint report maize production in 1996/97 would reach 2.22 million tonnes compared to 2.7 million tonnes in 1995/96.

"This decline reflects both lower planting and yields. As a result of low farm gate prices in 1995, some farmers in the main producing areas reduced long-rains maize planting in favour of increased wheat cultivation," the joint report said.
"Reduced use of fertiliser and high-quality seed, a decision spurred by high-input prices, negatively affected yields," added the report, issued in the Kenyan capital.

The report said "As a result of the failure of the rains in some provinces, it is estimated that 1.6 million individuals immediately require relief assistance in the drought-stressed areas until the next harvest in February 1997."
The report did not give the size of maize requirements.
Wheat production was expected to increase 12 percent in 1996/97 to 350,000 tonnes, the report said.

The report said that in the eastern, coast and northeast provinces and some parts of central province, rains failed for a second year and the food situation was tight. It said affected areas required swift action to avert a serious food crisis.
The Famine Early Warning System (FEWS) said in a November report that worst-affected pastoralists in the northern areas would lose the remaining animals in their milk herds.
Nairobi newspapers said this week that South African planes were flying emergency relief to the northern region.

Thursday's report said lower production required the government to lift a two-year-old ban on maize imports imposed in 1995 and start forward-planning to give traders "the right economic signals" to ensure import needs were met in April 1997.
